newsitem.title: USA: Jury convicts talk show guest of 2nd degree murder.
newsitem.headline: Jury convicts talk show guest of 2nd degree murder.

text.p: A jury Tuesday found a "Jenny Jones" talk show guest guilty of second-degree murder for killing another man who revealed a crush on him during the taping of the nationally syndicated TV show.
Jonathan Schmitz, 26, blinked as the verdict was read but showed little emotion as he was led away in handcuffs. Sentencing was scheduled for Dec. 4.

In reaching the verdict, the jury decided that Schmitz did not commit premeditated first degree murder in the death of Scott Amedure as initially charged, making it likely that he will not spend the rest of his life in prison.

First degree murder carries a mandatory life sentence in Michigan, but those convicted of second-degree murder can receive any number of years up to life in prison. Most second degree murder convicts in Michigan serve less than 20 years, according to the state's Department of Corrections.
The jury also convicted Schmitz on a felony firearm charge that carries a two-year sentence.
Schmitz admitted shooting Amedure, 32, with a shotgun on March 9, 1995, three days after Amedure revealed during a taping of the show in Chicago that he had a crush on Schmitz.
Members of Amedure's family were upset with the verdict, but grateful that the jury did not opt for lesser charges for Schmitz, including two misdemeanors.

"There's no way that he's going to end up getting enough time to justify what happened to Scott," said Amedure's brother, Frank. "Scott's gone forever and he'll be lucky to do 20 years. He'll be out when he's 46 years old, and that's not fair."

Amedure said his family intends to pursue a $25 million lawsuit against the show, host Jenny Jones and producer Telepictures, a unit of Warner Brothers. The family has hired Geoffrey Fieger, the outspoken lawyer of assisted suicide activist Jack Kevorkian, to try the case.
"None of this would have happened but for the Jenny Jones show exploiting homosexuality as a sensitive issue," Frank Amedure said.

Some jurors said they decided on the second degree murder conviction because they believed a key element of Schmitz' defence -- that the humiliation he suffered from the show, coupled with a history of mental illnesses, drinking and emotional problems, rendered him incapable of forming the intent needed for first degree murder.

"We saw this show as a catalyst in a young man's life who's already had emotional problems," juror Joyce O'Brien told reporters. "When the show came, it was a catalyst that threw him back into an emotional tailspin."

On Friday jurors were deadlocked, with 10 of 12 voting to convict Schmitz of first degree murder. But juror Joseph Wurm said all 12 believed prosecutors had proven the elements needed for second degree murder -- that Schmitz caused Amedure's death and intended to kill him or place him in grave danger, without premeditation.

The show in question was never aired, but it was replayed for the jury and portions of it were repeated on television newscasts. In it, Schmitz appeared surprised when Amedure, an acquaintance and neighbour, revealed his affections.
Schmitz, seen laughing and then burying his face in his hands, told the studio audience he was not homosexual.

During the trial a producer for the show admitted that she misled Schmitz into believing his admirer could have been a woman in order to persuade him to appear on the show, but said she also told him the admirer might be a man.
But jurors said the trial's major highlight, the testimony of talk show host Jones, provided them with little insight.

Jones, a vivacious, quick-witted diva in front of the camera, was timid on the stand, saying she knew little about the inner workings of her show and the chain of events that led up to Amedure's revelation of his affections for Schmitz.

Defence attorney James Burdick said he plans to appeal the verdict on grounds that several pieces of evidence, including photos of Amedure's shotgun wounds, should not have been shown to jurors because they were irrelevant.

"Jonathan Schmitz is of course very guilt-ridden by what happened, but that doesn't ignore the fact that Jonathan Schmitz did not have the capacity to make those decisions on that day," Burdick said. "His mind cannot grasp what occurred that day, yet."
